name: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAA)
short: ALS trial stopped: more deaths (24 BCAA vs 13 placebo); another: faster lung decline, maybe chance, harm not ruled out. Liver trials (8 of 18 into a vein): nausea, diarrhoea 12% vs 3%, very uncertain.
text: In people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, motor neuron disease), a placebo-controlled trial of daily L-leucine 12 g, L-isoleucine 6 g and L-valine 6 g was stopped by its data monitoring committee after 126 patients had been recruited, because of excess deaths in the BCAA group (24 versus 13 with placebo) together with a lack of benefit. In another 6-month placebo-controlled ALS trial in 95 patients, the decline in lung function (forced vital capacity) was about 2.5 times greater with BCAA or L-threonine than with placebo; the authors said this may have been due to chance but that an adverse effect could not be ruled out, while also describing the amino acids as well tolerated. A Cochrane review that identified six eligible amino acid trials in ALS, two of which were excluded from analysis, found no survival benefit and described adverse events with BCAA as comparable to those with the control treatment; Cochrane withdrew this review in 2008, and the withdrawn record gives no reason. In liver disease, a 2026 Cochrane review of 18 randomised trials (10 of oral and 8 of intravenous BCAA) with 934 adults with hepatic encephalopathy, nearly all with cirrhosis, found that BCAA may have little to no effect on deaths from any cause, with very uncertain evidence; in the six studies that reported them, nausea and diarrhoea, counted as serious adverse events, occurred in 58 of 477 participants (12%) given BCAA and 16 of 538 (3%) in control groups given diets, but the pooled estimate was very uncertain (risk ratio 2.05, 95% CI 0.40 to 10.58). A systematic review of 54 studies of BCAA supplementation in chronic liver disease, almost all at high or serious risk of bias, found that no study reported serious side effects and concluded that preventive BCAA supplementation appears safe in cirrhosis. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
